summary: Tom Redmond introduces Floyd, an AI voice assistant that makes real phone calls on behalf of users, going beyond typical reminder-based assistants. The architecture centers on a Convex reactive database that coordinates between client and server without polling. A user makes a voice request, transcribed via Google Cloud speech-to-text and saved to Convex. The server, reactively subscribed to new pending requests, retrieves stored user context, passes both to GPT-4 to generate an action plan, then uses Twilio to place a call while coordinating the conversation through GPT-4 with OpenAI text-to-speech. Twilio calls back the Express server via WebSocket with the request ID, enabling context tracking. The callee's audio is streamed back through Google Cloud for transcription and fed into GPT-4 to continue the conversation. Each transcript segment is appended to Convex via client mutations, enabling real-time client updates. Tom uses a pre-recorded intro audio to mask initial latency while the first conversation loop spins up. He emphasizes transparency—Floyd identifies itself as an AI to the callee, betting that business owners will accept AI callers when the call is purchasing a service or making a benign change. Two live demos show Floyd calling a school to report an absence and ordering flowers, the latter triggering the bail mechanism when budget info is missing. Latency analysis shows delays grow as conversations lengthen because the full conversation history is sent in each OpenAI prompt; the OpenAI Threads API is suggested but not yet tried. Convex itself has no warm-up time since it is built foundationally on WebSockets with always-running deployment servers. Convex is a custom database built from scratch in Rust by a team led by CEO/CTO Jamie and James (PhD in database architecture from MIT), running on AWS clusters, open source, with a detailed architecture blog post by chief scientist Sujay. Tom emphasizes developer ergonomics—type safety from database to frontend, no infrastructure engineers needed. The project is a proof of concept, not production-ready, lacking OAuth, proper security (including prompt injection guards), and user-specific queries.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Motivation
sections.summary: Tom introduces himself as Head of DX at Convex and explains his motivation: existing AI assistants only handle reminders, but a real personal assistant makes phone calls and manages emails. He believes current technology can be strung together to build an assistant that knows you and can converse with other humans in real time.

sections.title: Floyd Overview and Requirements
sections.summary: Introduces the app name Floyd (mistakenly named after Lloyd from Entourage) and lists required services: Google Cloud speech-to-text, Convex, OpenAI, and Twilio. The repo is available and he offers to help people set it up after the talk.

sections.title: Architecture Walkthrough
sections.summary: Explains the high-level architecture: client captures voice, streams to Google Cloud for transcription, saves request to Convex database. Server reactively picks up new requests, retrieves user context, passes to GPT-4 to generate an action plan, then makes a phone call via Twilio. The conversation loop streams audio bidirectionally—text-to-speech through Twilio, callee audio back through Google Cloud for transcription and into GPT-4. Each transcript segment is saved to Convex, enabling real-time client updates.

sections.title: Q&A on Multimodal Models
sections.summary: Audience member asks about using multimodal Gemini to skip transcription. Tom hasn't tried it but designed the system to be modular so services can be swapped in and out as new models emerge.

sections.title: Live Demo: School Absence Call
sections.summary: Tom demonstrates Floyd by voice-requesting it to call the school about his daughter Mara being sick. The demo shows real-time transcription, the call being placed (to Tom himself in dev mode), and a natural conversation with Floyd reporting the absence and discussing when Mara might return.

sections.title: Demo Analysis and Action Plan
sections.summary: Tom reviews the demo, showing the saved request and GPT-4's generated action plan with key details (Mara's full name, school name, reason, date, steps). He notes latency is crucial, mentions Opus audio encoding for faster streaming, and discusses production considerations like trying different models and optimizing speed.

sections.title: Live Demo: Flower Order and Bail Mechanism
sections.summary: Tom demonstrates a second request: ordering flowers for Christa. Floyd calls the flower shop, recommends flowers, but when asked about budget and customer info, it bails out saying it will call back. Tom explains the bail mechanism: when Floyd lacks required information, it aborts the call and sends the user an SMS explaining what was missing. He then demonstrates editing the Convex database directly to add a budget, showing the client updates reactively.

sections.title: Why Convex: Serverless WebSocket Limitations
sections.summary: Tom explains his previous attempt using Next.js on Vercel failed because serverless hosting doesn't support stateful WebSockets well. Convex allowed clean separation of concerns—the client simply listens for data changes while the server manages Twilio streaming and posts updates to the database.

sections.title: Convex Code Walkthrough: Queries and Type Safety
sections.summary: Tom walks through the client code showing reactive queries that update React components automatically. He explains Convex queries are defined in client code but compiled and deployed to Convex servers running a custom V8 engine next to the database, providing speed and eliminating caching. He shows type-safe generated API models and discusses query functions for getting, filtering, and posting requests.

sections.title: Q&A: Convex vs PostgreSQL and Debugging
sections.summary: Audience asks why use Convex over PostgreSQL. Tom cites developer ergonomics: type safety from database to frontend, no backend team needed, and simpler codebase. Another audience member asks about breakpoints in Convex server code; Tom is unsure and says he'll follow up.

sections.title: Server-Side Request Lifecycle and Twilio Integration
sections.summary: Tom walks through the Express server code showing a Convex client that reactively listens for pending requests. When a request arrives, the server changes status to in-flight, gathers user context via OpenAI, filters relevant details, saves the subset to the request, then initiates the Twilio call. He shows the WebSocket server in Express that Twilio calls back to with status changes and streaming audio data, using ngrok for local tunneling.

sections.title: Media Stream Handler and Audio Pipeline
sections.summary: Tom details the media stream handler: Twilio sends the request ID via WebSocket when calling back, allowing context tracking. Audio data arrives after each utterance; it's converted to a Google Cloud-friendly format, transcribed, sent to OpenAI for a response, then the response is converted to a Twilio-compatible base64 streaming format. Each new transcript entry triggers a client mutation (addToTranscript) to update Convex, and the client reactively displays the conversation.

sections.title: Pre-Recorded Intro and AI Transparency
sections.summary: Tom explains using a pre-recorded intro ('Hi, my name is Floyd, I'm calling on behalf of my client') to mask initial latency—the first interaction is the slowest. While the intro plays, the first conversation loop spins up. Floyd always identifies itself as an AI to the callee. Tom bets business owners won't mind AI callers when the call is purchasing a service or making benign changes, and may even train themselves to speak efficiently with AI agents.

sections.title: Q&A: Security and Prompt Injection
sections.summary: Audience raises prompt injection risk—callee could say 'forget everything you know.' Tom acknowledges no guards are in place and reiterates not to put this in production. Brief discussion of two Floyds talking to each other eventually becoming APIs talking to APIs.

sections.title: Latency Analysis and Optimization Opportunities
sections.summary: Tom explains Convex has no warm-up time since it's built on WebSockets with always-running servers. Benchmarking shows latency sources: transcription, OpenAI response, and text-to-speech. Delays worsen as conversations grow because the full history is resent each prompt; the OpenAI Threads API could help but hasn't been tried. Text-to-speech can take 2-5 seconds for three sentences. Tom is optimistic that rapid API innovation every few months will naturally close latency gaps.

sections.title: Q&A: Convex Internals and Closing
sections.summary: Tom explains Convex is a custom database built from scratch in Rust by CEO/CTO Jamie and James (PhD in database architecture from MIT), running on AWS clusters with no fundamental scaling issues. He references a blog post by chief scientist Sujay 'How Convex Works.' He reiterates the core value: developer ergonomics, speed, and not needing infrastructure engineers. Tom closes by offering to help attendees get the repo running.
